current_example.title: Example: Calculating the Derivative of a Function of Three Intermediate Variables and Two Independent Variables

q-95083.name: Question 1
q-95083.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14142932/assets/7e5b5001794ecdf2c9b9e9102f334a63d2c59bc6f7511c2eb7fa358fc94cb0c5.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $s,$ where $x=x(s)$ and $y=y(s),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=y{e}^{x},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}={e}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =s{e}^{\sqrt{s}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & ={e}^{\sqrt{s}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{s}},\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s} \\  & =s{e}^{\sqrt{s}}\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{s}}+{e}^{\sqrt{s}}\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{s}}{2}{e}^{\sqrt{s}}+{e}^{\sqrt{s}} \\  & =(1+\frac{\sqrt{s}}{2}){e}^{\sqrt{s}}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-95083.html:
Question 1
?

If f(x,y)=yex, x=s and y=s, compute dfds for s>0.

a
(1+s)es
b
(1+12s)es
c
(1+s2)es
d
(1+1s)es
e
(2+s)es
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) with one independent variable s, where x=x(s) and y=y(s), can be expressed as follows:

dfds=∂f∂x⋅dxds+∂f∂y⋅dyds

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y:

∂f∂x=yex,∂f∂y=ex

Writing the above results in terms of s, we get

∂f∂x=ses,∂f∂y=es.

Next, we take the derivatives of x and y with respect to s, and we get

dxds=12s,dyds=1.

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

dfds=∂f∂x⋅dxds+∂f∂y⋅dyds=ses⋅12s+es⋅1=s2es+es=(1+s2)es.

q-95076.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14142932/assets/f01b253f560405a8c0f4be8f8797c652fb0ddf774f4db110b8822313b8ac50f3.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $t,$ where $x=x(t)$ and $y=y(t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x{e}^{y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}={x}^{2}{e}^{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2(2t){e}^{{t}^{2}}=4t{e}^{{t}^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =(2t)^{2}{e}^{{t}^{2}}=4{t}^{2}{e}^{{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=2,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \\  & =4t{e}^{{t}^{2}}\cdot 2+4{t}^{2}{e}^{{t}^{2}}\cdot 2t \\  & =8t{e}^{{t}^{2}}+8{t}^{3}{e}^{{t}^{2}} \\  & =8t(1+{t}^{2}){e}^{{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-95076.html:
Question 2
?

If f(x,y)=x2ey,x=2t and y=t2, compute dfdt.

a
4t(1+2t)et2
b
 2t2(1+t2)et2
c
8t(1+t2)et2
d
8t3(2+t)et2
e
4t(2+t)et2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) with one independent variable t, where x=x(t) and y=y(t), can be expressed as follows:

dfdt=∂f∂x⋅dxdt+∂f∂y⋅dydt

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y:

∂f∂x=2xey,∂f∂y=x2ey

Writing the above results in terms of t, we get

∂f∂x=2(2t)et2=4tet2,∂f∂y=(2t)2et2=4t2et2.

Next, we take the derivatives of x and y with respect to t, and we get

dxdt=2,dydt=2t.

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

dfdt=∂f∂x⋅dxdt+∂f∂y⋅dydt=4tet2⋅2+4t2et2⋅2t=8tet2+8t3et2=8t(1+t2)et2.

q-170671.name: Question 3
q-170671.worked_solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=(1-{y}^{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-2y\operatorname{sin}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =(1-{cos}^{2}⁡x)\operatorname{cos}⁡x={sin}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-2\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & ={sin}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x+(-2\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x+2{sin}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\  & =3{sin}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

If f(x,y)=(1−y2)sin⁡x and y=cos⁡x, compute dfdx.

a
−3sin⁡xcos2⁡x
b
sin⁡xcos⁡x
c
sin⁡xcos2⁡x
d
sin2⁡xcos⁡x
e
3sin2⁡xcos⁡x
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) in the case where y=y(x) can be expressed as follows:

dfdx=∂f∂x+∂f∂y⋅dydx

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y:

∂f∂x=(1−y2)cos⁡x,∂f∂y=−2ysin⁡x

Writing the above results in terms of x, we get

∂f∂x=(1−cos2⁡x)cos⁡x=sin2⁡xcos⁡x,∂f∂y=−2cos⁡xsin⁡x

Next, we take the derivative y with respect to x, and we get

dydx=−sin⁡x.

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

dfdx=sin2⁡xcos⁡x+(−2cos⁡xsin⁡x)⋅(−sin⁡x)=sin2⁡xcos⁡x+2sin2⁡xcos⁡x=3sin2⁡xcos⁡x.

\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-2x\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+y),\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+y)\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =-2x\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{x}), \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{x}).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =-2x\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{x})+(-\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{x}))\cdot (-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}) \\  & =(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}-2x)\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{x}) \\  & =(\frac{1-2{x}^{3}}{{x}^{2}})\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{{x}^{3}+1}{x}).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

If f(x,y)=cos⁡(x2+y) and y=1x, compute dfdx.

a
(2x2+1x)sin⁡(x3+1x)
b
(1−3x3)sin⁡(x2+1x2)
c
(1−2x3x2)sin⁡(x3+1x)
d
(1−4x3x)cos⁡(x3+1x2)
e
(1+4x2)cos⁡(x2−1x)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) in the case where y=y(x) can be expressed as follows: dfdx=∂f∂x+∂f∂y⋅dydx

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y: ∂f∂x=−2xsin⁡(x2+y),∂f∂y=−sin⁡(x2+y)

Writing the above results in terms of x, we get ∂f∂x=−2xsin⁡(x2+1x),∂f∂y=−sin⁡(x2+1x).

Next, we take the derivative y with respect to x, and we get dydx=−1x2.

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get dfdx=−2xsin⁡(x2+1x)+(−sin⁡(x2+1x))⋅(−1x2)=(1x2−2x)sin⁡(x2+1x)=(1−2x3x2)sin⁡(x3+1x).

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y=y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2xy,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}={x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2(ts)(s-t)=2t{s}^{2}-2s{t}^{2}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =(ts)^{2}={t}^{2}{s}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂t} & =s, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂t} & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) with two independent variables s and t, where x=x(s,t) and y=y(s,t), can be expressed as follows: ∂f∂t=∂f∂x⋅∂x∂t+∂f∂y⋅∂y∂t

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y: ∂f∂x=2xy,∂f∂y=x2

Writing the above results in terms of s and t, we get ∂f∂x=2(ts)(s−t)=2ts2−2st2,∂f∂y=(ts)2=t2s2.

Next, we take the derivatives of x and y with respect to t, and we get ∂x∂t=s,∂y∂t=−1.

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get ∂f∂t=∂f∂x⋅∂x∂t+∂f∂y⋅∂y∂t=(2ts2−2st2)(s)+(t2s2)(−1)=2ts3−2s2t2−t2s2=2ts3−3t2s2=ts2(2s−3t).

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y=y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=1,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-1\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =1, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡t, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s} \\  & =(1)(-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)+(-1)(\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =-(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y,z)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t)$ and $z=z(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x,y$ and $z:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2xy,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}={x}^{2}-5z,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=-5y.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2(st)({s}^{3})=2{s}^{4}t, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =(st)^{2}-5(s\operatorname{sin}⁡t)={s}^{2}{t}^{2}-5s\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =-5{s}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & =t, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =3{s}^{2}, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂s} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =(2{s}^{4}t)\cdot t+({s}^{2}{t}^{2}-5s\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot 3{s}^{2}+(-5{s}^{3})\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t \\  & =2{s}^{4}{t}^{2}+3{s}^{4}{t}^{2}-15{s}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t-5{s}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\  & =5{s}^{4}{t}^{2}-20{s}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y,z)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t)$ and $z=z(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂s}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=2z.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2(t+2s)=2t+4s, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =2(3t-s)=6t-2s, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =2st.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & =2, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =-1, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂s} & =t.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =(2t+4s)\cdot 2+(6t-2s)\cdot (-1)+(2st)\cdot t \\  & =4t+8s-6t+2s+2s{t}^{2} \\  & =10s-2t+2s{t}^{2} \\  & =2(5s-t+s{t}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 8

Let f(x,y,z)=x2+y2+z2, where x=t+2s, y=3t−s and z=st. Calculate ∂f∂s.

a
t(5−s)2
b
s(t+s)2
c
3s−5t−1
d
4(st+s−t)
e
2(5s−t+st2)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y,z) with two independent variables s and t, where x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t) and z=z(s,t), can be expressed as follows: ∂f∂s=∂f∂x⋅∂x∂s+∂f∂y⋅∂y∂s+∂f∂z⋅∂z∂s

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x,y and z: ∂f∂x=2x,∂f∂y=2y,∂f∂z=2z.

Writing the above results in terms of s and t, we get ∂f∂x=2(t+2s)=2t+4s,∂f∂y=2(3t−s)=6t−2s,∂f∂z=2st.

Next, we take the derivatives of x, y, and z with respect to s, and we get ∂x∂s=2,∂y∂s=−1,∂z∂s=t.

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get ∂f∂s=(2t+4s)⋅2+(6t−2s)⋅(−1)+(2st)⋅t=4t+8s−6t+2s+2st2=10s−2t+2st2=2(5s−t+st2).
